content: Preterm birth is a significant cause of perinatal mortality and morbidity, affecting approximately 9% of births in high-income countries and 13% in lowand middle-income countries. Tocolytic drugs are used to suppress uterine contractions in women experiencing preterm labor. Among these, betamimetics are the most commonly used but are associated with frequent and sometimes severe maternal side effects. Calcium channel blockers (CCBs), such as nifedipine, may offer similar efficacy in delaying labor with fewer side effects compared to betamimetics. Oxytocin receptor antagonists (ORAs), such as atosiban, also have a low side-effect profile. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of CCBs, used as tocolytic agents, on maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes in women experiencing preterm labor. The analysis included all randomized trials, both published and unpublished, where CCBs were used for tocolysis in women between 20 and 36 weeks of gestation. Data were collected and analyzed independently by two reviewers, with results presented as risk ratios (RR) for categorical data and mean differences (MD) for continuous data, along with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The number needed to treat to benefit (NNTB) and the number needed to treat to harm (NNTH) were calculated for statistically significant categorical outcomes. This review incorporated 26 additional trials, bringing the total to 38 trials involving 3,550 women. Of these, 35 trials used nifedipine as the CCB, while three used nicardipine. Only one trial employed blinding of the intervention and outcome assessment, but objective outcomes such as timing of birth and perinatal mortality were considered to have a low risk of detection bias. Two small trials comparing CCBs with placebo or no treatment demonstrated a significant reduction in births occurring within 48 hours of trial entry (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.43) but also showed an increase in maternal adverse effects (RR 49.89, 95% CI 3.13 to 795.02, based on one trial of 89 women). Due to substantial heterogeneity, data on preterm birth before 37 weeks were not combined. One placebo-controlled trial showed no difference (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.03), while another non-placebo-controlled trial reported a reduction (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.62). No other outcomes were reported in these trials. When comparing CCBs (mainly nifedipine) with other tocolytics, including betamimetics, glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) patches, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), magnesium sulfate, and ORAs, no significant reductions were observed in primary outcomes such as birth within 48 hours of treatment or perinatal mortality. However, compared to betamimetics, CCBs were associated with fewer maternal adverse effects (average RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.53) and fewer maternal adverse effects requiring discontinuation of therapy (average RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.48). CCBs also increased the interval between trial entry and birth (average MD 4.38 days, 95% CI 0.25 to 8.52) and gestational age at delivery (MD 0.71 weeks, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.09). Additionally, CCBs reduced the rates of preterm birth (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.98), very preterm birth (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.93), respiratory distress syndrome (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.86), necrotizing enterocolitis (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.96), intraventricular hemorrhage (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.84), neonatal jaundice (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.92), and admissions to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) (average RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.87). No differences were observed in long-term outcomes assessed at nine to twelve years of age. When comparing CCBs with ORAs, data from one blinded study showed that CCBs increased gestational age at birth (MD 1.20 weeks, 95% CI 0.25 to 2.15) and reduced rates of preterm birth (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.89), NICU admissions (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.85), and NICU stay duration (MD -5.40 days, 95% CI -10.84 to 0.04). However, maternal adverse effects were more frequent in the CCB group (average RR 2.61, 95% CI 1.43 to 4.74). Compared to magnesium sulfate, CCBs were associated with fewer maternal adverse effects (average RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.68) and shorter NICU stays (MD -4.55 days, 95% CI -8.17 to -0.92). No significant differences were observed in comparisons with GTN patches or NSAIDs, although the sample sizes were small. Similarly, no differences were evident in trials comparing nicardipine with other tocolytics, though the limited data preclude strong conclusions. A small trial comparing higherversus lower-dose nifedipine showed no significant differences, although some measures of neonatal morbidity tended to favor the higher dose. In conclusion, CCBs, particularly nifedipine, appear to offer benefits over placebo or no treatment in delaying birth, potentially allowing time for antenatal corticosteroid administration and transfer to higher-level care. CCBs also demonstrated advantages over betamimetics in terms of pregnancy prolongation, reduced neonatal morbidity, and fewer maternal adverse effects. While CCBs may have some benefits over ORAs and magnesium sulfate, ORAs were associated with fewer maternal adverse effects. Importantly, no differences were observed in perinatal mortality, and data on long-term outcomes remain limited. The lack of blinding in most trials weakens the strength of the evidence. Further well-designed trials are needed to evaluate the shortand long-term benefits of CCBs compared to placebo, no treatment, and other tocolytics, particularly ORAs. Future research should also focus on identifying optimal dosing regimens and formulations of CCBs and should include blinded interventions, assessments of long-term outcomes into early childhood, and cost analyses.
